passages.t: A shadow of the good things to come
passages.happening:
“For the law is only a shadow of the good things to come, not the realities themselves. It can never, by the same sacrifices offered year after year, make perfect those who draw near to worship” (verse 1).

“If it could, would not the offerings have ceased? For the worshipers would have been cleansed once for all, and would no longer have felt the guilt of their sins. Instead, those sacrifices are an annual reminder of sins, because it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (verses 2-4).
passages.hearers:
This is the last step of the long teaching that began in chapter 8.

‘Shadow’ again. A shadow has the shape of what casts it, but it is not the thing itself. The law gave the true shape of what God would do, but not the full reality, which is Christ.

The writer's argument is from repetition. The Day of Atonement came every year. If one year's sacrifice had cleansed the worshippers for good, there would have been no need for the next. The very repeating showed that the work was not finished. Each year the sacrifices reminded people of their sins.

There is a contrast hidden here with the Lord's Supper. The word for ‘reminder’ is the word Jesus used at the Last Supper, ‘in remembrance of Me’ (Luke 22:19). The old rite kept sins in memory. The new meal keeps Christ's sacrifice in memory.

‘Impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.’ An animal cannot stand in the place of a person. Its blood could cleanse the body for worship, as chapter 9 said, but it could not by itself remove the guilt of the heart.
passages.ot:
The prophets of Israel had already said that animal sacrifices were not what God most wanted. “‘What good to Me is your multitude of sacrifices?’ says the LORD” (Isaiah 1:11). “For I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings” (Hosea 6:6). Samuel told King Saul, “Behold, obedience is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22).

These prophets were not rejecting the sacrifices God had given. They were rejecting sacrifice without a changed heart. And they show that Israel's own Scriptures already looked for something deeper than the offering of animals. The next verses quote one more such passage, Psalm 40.
passages.hard:
‘Impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.’ Was Israel's worship useless, and were Israelites not forgiven?

No. Leviticus promises that through the sacrifices ‘they will be forgiven’ (Leviticus 4:20), and Israel's faithful knew God's forgiveness, as the psalms sing. Hebrews does not deny that. It says where the forgiveness finally came from: Christ's death redeemed people ‘from the transgressions committed under the first covenant’ (9:15). The sacrifices were God's own gift, teaching his people that sin is costly and that he provides the way back, and pointing ahead to the one sacrifice that would fulfil them. The note on 9:1-10 says more.

For centuries some Christians used this letter, with other parts of the New Testament, to teach contempt for Jews and Judaism. That reading is false. This site rejects it. The note on Acts 2:22-28 sets out why.
passages.asks: The old sacrifices were a yearly reminder of sin. Ask whether your faith is mostly a reminder of your failures, or a remembrance of Christ's finished work. Ask what guilt you keep feeling that he has already taken away. And ask whether you come to the Lord's Supper remembering him.

passages.happening:
“Therefore, when Christ came into the world, He said: ‘Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but a body You prepared for Me. In burnt offerings and sin offerings You took no delight. Then I said, ‘Here I am, it is written about Me in the scroll: I have come to do Your will, O God.’’” (verses 5-7).

The writer explains. First the psalm says God did not desire the sacrifices “(although they are offered according to the law)” (verse 8). “Then He adds, ‘Here I am, I have come to do Your will.’ He takes away the first to establish the second” (verse 9).

“And by that will, we have been sanctified through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
The writer hears Psalm 40 as the words of Christ at his coming into the world. It is as if the Son, about to be born, speaks to the Father: the old sacrifices could not do it, so you have prepared a body for me, and I have come to do your will.

The contrast in the psalm is between sacrifice and obedience. God wanted more than animals. He wanted a whole life given to him in obedience. Jesus gave that, in a real human body, and then gave that body on the cross.

‘He takes away the first to establish the second’ means: the system of animal sacrifices is set aside, and the obedience of Christ takes its place as the way God's will is done.

‘Sanctified’ means set apart for God and made fit to come near him, as priests and holy vessels were set apart. Believers are made holy ‘through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all’. The full name, ‘Jesus Christ’, is rare in Hebrews, and it stands here at the climax.
passages.ot:
Verses 5 to 7 quote Psalm 40:6-8. In the Berean Standard Bible, which translates the Hebrew, it reads: “Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but my ears You have opened. Burnt offerings and sin offerings You did not require. Then I said, ‘Here I am, I have come— it is written about me in the scroll: I delight to do Your will, O my God; Your law is within my heart.’” (Psalm 40:6-8).

In its own setting it is the prayer of a man God had lifted out of a pit. He has learned that what God wants most is a life that listens and obeys. ‘Ears You have opened’ is a Hebrew way of saying ‘you have made me able to hear and obey’.

Hebrews quotes the Greek Old Testament, and here the difference matters. Where the Hebrew says ‘my ears You have opened’, the Greek reads “a body You prepared for Me”. No one knows for certain how the Greek reading arose. The site's note on Psalm 40 says that many readers see the two as meaning much the same, since ears are part of a body and both speak of a whole self given to God; others see a fuller meaning in the Greek, which Hebrews draws out. Hebrews' point does not hang on one word. It is that God wanted obedience more than animal sacrifice, and that Jesus gave it, in his body, once for all.
passages.hard:
Did God never want the sacrifices? Then why did he command them?

The psalm, like the prophets, is not saying that God never wanted the sacrifices he commanded. The law gave them, and Hebrews says they were ‘offered according to the law’ (verse 8). The psalm is saying that sacrifice was never the deepest thing God wanted. What he wanted was a heart that loves him and a life that obeys him: “Your law is within my heart” (Psalm 40:8). The sacrifices served that, and pointed to the one perfect obedience still to come.

And ‘He takes away the first to establish the second’ is about the sacrifices, not about the people who offered them. It is not a verdict on the Jewish people. The book page's part on the old covenant and the Jewish people says more.
passages.asks: Jesus came saying, ‘Here I am, I have come to do Your will.’ Ask whether you have said those words to God with your own life. Ask what God wants from you more than outward religion. And ask what it means to be made holy by the body of Jesus, given once for all.

passages.happening:
“Day after day every priest stands to minister and to offer again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God. Since that time, He waits for His enemies to be made a footstool for His feet, because by a single offering He has made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified” (verses 11-14).

“The Holy Spirit also testifies to us about this” (verse 15). The writer quotes Jeremiah again: “I will put My laws in their hearts and inscribe them on their minds”, and “Their sins and lawless acts I will remember no more” (verses 16-17).

“And where these have been forgiven, an offering for sin is no longer needed” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Picture the scene. In the tabernacle there was no chair for the priests. They stood, because their work was never done. Day after day the same sacrifices. Christ offered one sacrifice and sat down. A seated priest means a finished work.

He ‘waits’ now for his enemies to be put under his feet, as Psalm 110 promised. The victory is won; its full showing is still to come.

‘He has made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified.’ Two things are true together. What Christ did is complete: his people are made perfect, brought to God, for all time. And they are ‘being sanctified’, growing in holiness day by day. Believers live between what is finished and what is still being worked out.

The writer closes the whole argument where he began it in chapter 8, with Jeremiah's promise: God will remember their sins no more. And if sins are truly forgiven, no more offering is needed. Verse 18 is like a verdict at the end of a trial.
passages.ot:
Verse 13 takes up the second half of Psalm 110:1, “until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet” (Psalm 110:1).

Verses 16 and 17 quote Jeremiah 31:33-34 again, in a shorter form: “I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts” and “I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more” (Jeremiah 31:33-34). In its own setting it is God's promise to Israel and Judah after the exile, as the note on 8:7-13 explains.
passages.asks: Christ sat down because the work was finished. Ask whether you live as though your forgiveness still depends on your own sacrifices. Ask what it means that you are both ‘made perfect for all time’ and ‘being sanctified’. And ask whether you can rest in a verdict God has already given: no more offering is needed.

passages.t: Draw near, hold on, and meet together
passages.happening:
Now the writer turns from teaching to urging.

“Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body, and since we have a great priest over the house of God, let us draw near with a sincere heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled to cleanse us from a guilty conscience and our bodies washed with pure water” (verses 19-22).

“Let us hold resolutely to the hope we profess, for He who promised is faithful” (verse 23).

“And let us consider how to spur one another on to love and good deeds. Let us not neglect meeting together, as some have made a habit, but let us encourage one another, and all the more as you see the Day approaching” (verses 24-25).
passages.hearers:
In Greek, verses 19 to 25 are one long sentence. It begins with what we have, and then says what we should do.

What we have: confidence to enter the Most Holy Place, where only the high priest went once a year. A ‘new and living way’ through the curtain. And a great priest over God's household.

What we should do comes in three calls. ‘Let us draw near’: come to God, with a sincere heart and full trust. ‘Hearts sprinkled’ and ‘bodies washed’ use the language of priests being set apart for service; many readers hear in ‘bodies washed with pure water’ a reference to baptism. ‘Let us hold resolutely to the hope’: do not let go, because God keeps his promises. ‘Let us consider how to spur one another on’: think about each other, and stir each other up to love.

‘Spur’ translates a word that usually meant a sharp quarrel. The writer uses it on purpose for a good kind of provoking: provoke one another to love.

‘Let us not neglect meeting together, as some have made a habit.’ Some of the readers had stopped coming to the gatherings, perhaps from fear of being seen with the believers, perhaps from tiredness. The writer does not scold them from a distance. He calls everyone to encourage one another, ‘all the more as you see the Day approaching’, the day of Christ's return.
passages.ot:
‘Sprinkled’ and ‘washed’ recall how Aaron and his sons were washed with water and set apart as priests (Exodus 29:4). The prophets promised a deeper cleansing: “I will also sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean” (Ezekiel 36:25).

‘A great priest’ is the Greek Old Testament's phrase for Israel's high priest.

Israel's Scriptures delight in God's people gathered together: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony!” (Psalm 133:1). And the psalm Hebrews has just quoted speaks of praise in the gathering: “I proclaim righteousness in the great assembly” (Psalm 40:9).
passages.hard:
‘Let us not neglect meeting together.’ What about people who have been hurt by a church?

This verse is a call to encouragement, not a club. It was written to weary believers who were drifting away, to call them back to people who would help them hold on. It is never a reason to shame someone who has stepped away from a place where they were harmed, or to force anyone back into danger.

If you have been harmed by a controlling leader or church, what was done was wrong, and it was not your fault. Being taken in by someone who seemed godly is not a sign of weak faith; the Corinthians were taken in too. You are free to step away and to tell someone you trust. If you were abused in other ways, or a crime was done, it should be reported to the authorities. A pastor or counsellor outside that church may help you sort out what happened. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

And the verse does not say that faith can be kept only by perfect attendance. Many believers cannot gather for a time, through illness, distance, work or danger. The heart of the verse is ‘encourage one another’. If you are far from other believers now, the call is to find, when you can and where it is safe, even a few people who will help you hold on.
passages.asks: Draw near, hold on, encourage one another. Ask which of the three you most need now. Ask who you are meeting with, and whether you help them hold on. And ask who you could ‘spur on’ to love this week, gently, as someone who needs the same.

passages.t: The fourth warning: no other sacrifice
passages.happening:
Then comes another solemn warning.

“If we deliberately go on sinning after we have received the knowledge of the truth, no further sacrifice for sins remains, but only a fearful expectation of judgment and of raging fire that will consume all adversaries” (verses 26-27).

“Anyone who rejected the law of Moses died without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much more severely do you think one deserves to be punished who has trampled on the Son of God, profaned the blood of the covenant that sanctified him, and insulted the Spirit of grace?” (verses 28-29).

“For we know Him who said, ‘Vengeance is Mine; I will repay,’ and again, ‘The Lord will judge His people.’ It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (verses 30-31).
passages.hearers:
This is the fourth of the letter's warnings, and it is close to the warning of chapter 6. Notice again the word ‘we’. The writer includes himself.

‘Deliberately’ stands first in the Greek for emphasis. ‘Go on sinning’ describes a continuing course, not a single fall. And verse 29 says what that course is. To ‘trample on the Son of God’ is to treat him with contempt. To profane ‘the blood of the covenant’ is to treat Christ's death as worthless. To insult ‘the Spirit of grace’ is to throw God's kindness back in his face.

The argument goes from lesser to greater again. Under the law of Moses, someone who turned to other gods, proven by witnesses, was put to death. If turning from God then was so serious, how much more turning from his Son.

‘The living God’ is a title the letter uses again and again. He is not an idea that can be ignored. He is alive.
passages.ot:
The law's rule on witnesses is in Deuteronomy: “On the testimony of two or three witnesses a man shall be put to death” (Deuteronomy 17:6). In its setting the case was a person who had served other gods.

The ‘raging fire’ echoes Isaiah: “The fire set for Your enemies will consume them!” (Isaiah 26:11). In Isaiah the fire falls on the enemies of God's people. Hebrews warns that those who turn against Christ from inside put themselves among the adversaries.

Verse 30 quotes the Song of Moses: “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay” (Deuteronomy 32:35), and “For the LORD will vindicate His people” (Deuteronomy 32:36). In the Song, God acts for his people against their enemies; in the Greek Old Testament the word reads ‘judge’, and Hebrews uses it to warn that God judges within his own household too. Paul quotes the same words to tell believers to leave revenge to God (Romans 12:19).

The law itself made the distinction this passage rests on. For a person who sinned without meaning to, a sacrifice was given and “he will be forgiven” (Numbers 15:28). “But the person who sins defiantly, whether a native or foreigner, blasphemes the LORD” (Numbers 15:30).
passages.hard:
‘If we deliberately go on sinning after we have received the knowledge of the truth, no further sacrifice for sins remains.’ Does this mean a believer who sins again is lost?

No. This verse is not about a believer who struggles with sin, falls, and comes back to God sorry. Everyone who follows Jesus sins and needs forgiveness again: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). ‘Go on sinning’ describes a continuing course, and verse 29 says what that course is: to trample on the Son of God, to treat the blood of the covenant as worthless, and to insult the Spirit of grace. It is a settled, deliberate turning against Christ himself. The law of Moses drew a similar line between sins done without meaning to and sins done ‘defiantly’ (Numbers 15:27-31). The logic is simple: Christ's sacrifice is the only one. To reject it is to have no other.

Christians read this warning through the same views as chapter 6. Much of the Reformed and Baptist world holds that those who finally turn against Christ in this way show they were never truly born again, though they belonged to the church; ‘the blood of the covenant that sanctified him’ is read as the outward setting apart of a member of God's people. Much of the Wesleyan and Arminian world holds that real believers can fall away by such deliberate turning from Christ. Others hold that the warning is one of the means God uses to keep his people from that end. Catholic and Orthodox teaching reads it as a warning about grave sin and turning from the faith, from which repentance is still possible by God's grace, though not by any other sacrifice. These notes do not choose. The note on Romans 8:31-39 and the Honest Answer, ‘Can you lose your salvation?’, set out the views.

And see how the passage ends: “But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed” (verse 39). The writer wants to keep his readers from walking away, not to drive tender consciences to despair.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The warning is spoken to ‘we’. Ask whether there is any part of you that has begun to treat Christ's death as a small thing. Ask what it means that God is ‘the living God’, not an idea you can set aside. And then read on to verse 39, and ask whether you can say with the writer, ‘we are not of those who shrink back’.

passages.t: Remember, and do not throw away your confidence
passages.happening:
The tone turns again, from warning to memory.

“Remember the early days that you were in the light. In those days, you endured a great conflict in the face of suffering. Sometimes you were publicly exposed to ridicule and persecution; at other times you were partners with those who were so treated. You sympathized with those in prison and joyfully accepted the confiscation of your property, knowing that you yourselves had a better and permanent possession” (verses 32-34).

“So do not throw away your confidence; it holds a great reward. You need to persevere, so that after you have done the will of God, you will receive what He has promised” (verses 35-36).

“For, ‘In just a little while, He who is coming will come and will not delay. But My righteous one will live by faith; and if he shrinks back, I will take no pleasure in him.’ But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls” (verses 37-39).
passages.hearers:
These verses give a glimpse of the readers' story. Soon after they came to faith, they were mocked in public, perhaps in the theatre where crowds gathered. Some were put in prison. In the Roman world, prisoners depended on friends to bring them food, and visiting a prisoner could mark you as one of his people. The readers did it anyway. Some lost their goods, taken by the authorities or by a mob. And they accepted it ‘joyfully’, because they knew they had something better that could not be taken.

Many who think the readers lived in Rome link these early sufferings with the time around AD 49, when the emperor Claudius ordered Jews to leave Rome, which Acts also mentions (Acts 18:2). Others think of other places and times. The letter does not say.

‘Do not throw away your confidence’ pictures a soldier throwing away his shield as he runs from battle. They had been brave before. They must not drop their shield now.

‘You need to persevere.’ Endurance means staying under a load without giving up. They need it ‘after you have done the will of God’, the will Jesus came to do (verse 7). They are to walk the road he walked.

Then a quotation about waiting and faith, and the last words of the chapter turn to the word ‘faith’, ready for chapter 11.
passages.ot:
Verses 37 and 38 join two passages. ‘In just a little while’ comes from Isaiah: “Hide yourselves a little while until the wrath has passed” (Isaiah 26:20).

The rest comes from Habakkuk. In the Berean Standard Bible, which translates the Hebrew, it reads: “For the vision awaits an appointed time; it testifies of the end and does not lie. Though it lingers, wait for it, since it will surely come and will not delay. Look at the proud one; his soul is not upright— but the righteous will live by faith—” (Habakkuk 2:3-4). In its own setting, the prophet had complained that God allowed evil to go on, and God told him to wait: the vision of God's justice would surely come, and the righteous person would live by faith, or faithfulness, while waiting.

Hebrews quotes the Greek Old Testament, which differs in several ways. In the Hebrew, what ‘will surely come’ is the vision; the Greek speaks of ‘He who is coming’, which Hebrews reads as the Messiah. The Hebrew's line about the proud one becomes, in the Greek, ‘if he shrinks back, I will take no pleasure in him’. And Hebrews puts the lines in a different order, so that the one who might shrink back is the righteous person himself. The effect is a warning to believers: the righteous live by faith, and shrinking back is the opposite of faith. Paul quotes the same line from Habakkuk, ‘The righteous will live by faith’ (Romans 1:17).
passages.hard:
‘Joyfully accepted the confiscation of your property.’ Does this mean Christians should accept every wrong done to them without complaint?

No. The readers lost their goods because they followed Christ, and they chose to bear it rather than deny him. That is the kind of suffering the writer praises. It is not a rule that anyone must stay where they are being hurt, or never seek justice, or never take help. Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. Paul himself appealed to the law to protect himself (Acts 25:11). And the readers' joy came from knowing they had ‘a better and permanent possession’, not from pretending the loss did not hurt.

If you are suffering now, for your faith or for any other reason, you do not have to carry it alone. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Remember the early days. Ask what God did for you when your faith was new, and what you were willing to give then. Ask where you are tempted to throw down your shield now. And ask what ‘better and permanent possession’ you are living for.
